narrative:
The model estimates a 45% chance that you will leave your current job. Because this probability is high enough to flag you as a likely departure, the organization has decided to deny your promotion.

The decision was driven primarily by three key aspects of your profile. First, having received other job offers while at your current employer was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward leaving. This suggests the model sees external opportunities as a clear signal that you may not stay long-term. Second, the length of time you have spent in your present role—6 to 10 years—worked in the opposite direction, pulling the prediction back toward staying; most employees the model expects to remain have shorter tenure here. Third, your overall career experience of 6 to 10 years also nudged the prediction upward toward leaving, as the typical employee flagged as likely to stay has either less or substantially more total experience.

Taken together, the combination of outside opportunities and your mid-range experience levels outweighed the stabilizing effect of your time at the organization, tipping the balance toward an expected departure.

You and your manager should discuss what would make staying more attractive. Reviewing your current compensation, recognition, and growth opportunities could reveal practical steps to reduce the risk of losing you. Addressing these areas now may change both your outlook and the model’s future assessment.
